items.mnemonic: Tongue tip flat on the back of your teeth – dental ta. A soft low curl resting on its stem – relaxed, while retroflex ट curls the tongue back to the roof of the mouth.
त (ta)'s breathy partner – tongue on the teeth plus one extra puff of breath: tha. The closed loop under the bar is a puffed cheek holding the extra air.
Dental da – tongue on the teeth, soft as the th in 'this'. A round belly with a small pointed elbow jutting left. Its curled-back cousin is ड (retroflex da).
द (da) + one puff of breath – dental dha. Watch out for घ (gha): ध leaves a small gap in its top bar and its loop narrows to a point; घ keeps a solid bar and a round curl.
Everyday na, tongue tip on the teeth like English n. Under the bar just one short kick onto the stem – त (ta) swings a big open curl, न stays minimal. Retroflex ण is the curled-back cousin.
Lips press together and pop open – pa. One clean open bowl hanging on the stem, nothing extra – the plainest of the lip letters.
प (pa) + one puff of breath – pha. The curl swinging off the right side of the stem is the puff of air escaping.
Lips together, voice buzzing – ba. A bowl on the stem with a short slash tucked inside the bowl – the slash is the buzz of the voice.
ब (ba) + one extra puff of breath – bha. No closed bowl here: a wing sweeps down to a point before the stem, and the top bar leaves a small gap – the gap lets the extra breath escape.
Humming ma – lips sealed, like m anywhere. The left stroke ties a small knot before the bowl and the top bar runs solid – भ (bha) skips the knot and breaks its bar.
ya as in yes. A smooth open swing into the stem – थ (tha)'s look-alike, but य leaves its loop open at the bottom; थ closes the circle.
ra – one quick tap of the tongue, lightly rolled. The smallest letter: a stem dropping from the bar with one leg kicking down-left.
la – tongue tip up, like English l. The tail dives under and curls back up, a ladle scooping to the left.
Halfway between v and w – soft va, lips barely touching. An empty bowl on the stem: ब (ba) minus the slash, and minus the buzz.
sha as in shoe – the everyday sh. A curled ribbon under the bar with a small slash through its tail.
प (pa) with a slash across its bowl – but it hisses: sha. In Hindi it sounds exactly like श; Sanskrit spelling decides which one a word uses.
sa as in sun. A little rollercoaster under the bar – curl, dip, stem – hissing as it slides.
ha – pure breath, as in hat. A curly hook with a small tail tucked under its chin, air spiraling out.
A vowel that simply sounds ri, as in ऋषि (rishi = sage). Body like र (ra) with an extra tail kicking out at the bottom left – a leftover from Sanskrit.
ज (ja) with a dot tucked underneath – the nukta. The dot loosens ja into a buzz: za as in zoo, for loanwords like ज़रूर (zaroor = definitely).
फ (pha) with a dot below – the nukta relaxes the lips into an English f: fa, as in फ़िल्म (film).
ड (retroflex da) with a dot below – start curled back, then flick the tongue tip forward as it lands: the flapped Ra of सड़क (saRak = road).
ढ (retroflex dha) with a dot – the same tongue-flick as ड़ plus one puff of breath: Rha, as in बूढ़ा (booRhaa = old).
ऋ's attached form – a tiny kinked hook under the letter: क + ृ = कृ (kri), as in कृपया (kripayaa = please). Don't confuse it with ु (u), a smoother curl.
One dot floating above the bar – the anusvara. Hum through the nose before the next consonant: हिंदी (hindee = Hindi) gets its n from this dot.
A tiny moon cradling a dot – the chandrabindu. It sends the whole vowel through your nose: हाँ (haan = yes). Moon + dot = a fuller nasal than the plain dot ं.
Two stacked dots after the letter – the visarga, a soft trailing puff of h. Rare outside Sanskrit loans like अतः (atah = therefore).
A small slash below – the halant. It deletes the consonant's built-in a: क says ka, क् is a bare k, ready to weld straight onto the next letter.
